newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin returns to busy agenda, political row.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin returns to busy agenda, political row.

text.p: A crowded work agenda and a nasty political row await Russian President Boris Yeltsin as he returns to work on Tuesday after the first rest in two years not forced upon him by ill health.
A year into his second term in office, Yeltsin appears to have left his heart problems behind him and have a firmer grip on power than ever.

In the latest sign of confidence, he announced on Monday that the rouble would be redenominated from January 1, 1998 -- a move aimed at breaking inflationary expectations which have become ingrained in Russians since market reforms began in 1992.
Yeltsin said no one would lose out when a new rouble worth 1,000 old ones is introduced.
He went on holiday in early July, dividing his time between northwestern Karelia and the central Samara region, and fishing in waters said by the media to have been specially stocked for him.

The Kremlin, which said at the weekend Yeltsin would return on Tuesday, had not previously announced how long he would stay on holiday, prompting some sources to speculate that the break would last to September.

The 66-year-old leader, who underwent quintuple heart bypass surgery last November, showed occasional signs of physical weakness before his holiday. But his entourage is now so sure of his health that it has fixed a busy schedule for him.

Yeltsin, who enjoys the international limelight, will visit Strasbourg, France on October 10 and 11 to address a Council of Europe summit. On November 10 he starts a visit to China, and travels to Sweden in December.

He has also ordered officials to start preparing an informal meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and is due to host German President Roman Herzog, the presidents of Egypt, France and the Philippines, and Italy's prime minister.
Less pleasant, but much more pressing, is Yeltsin's agenda closer to home.

He has already said he is thinking of inviting Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov to Moscow to try to break a deadlock over a political treaty. Moscow fought a disastrous war for nearly two years against breakaway Chechnya.

Yeltsin has also invited leaders of Georgia and its rebel region of Abkhazia to Moscow to try to push through a political deal between the two which will also decide the future of Russian peacekeepers in the area.

With Turkmenistan President Saparmurat Niyazov later this week he will discuss the tricky issue of the Caspian Sea and its natural resources, including oil. He is also expecting Armenian President Levon Ter-Petrosyan in August.
But, beyond doubt, the biggest immediate problem for the president is a ghastly row flaring between his supporters in the government and among banking tycoons.

The scandal which erupted after the partial privatisation of the Svyazinvest telecoms giant was the first serious test for top reformers in the government, namely first deputy prime ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov.

Up to now, no one has legally challenged the tender, which was won by a a consortium built around Uneximbank, Russia's third biggest bank, and backed by a number of powerful foreign invstors. The winners offered $1.875 billion against $1.71 billion offered by the other bidder.

But powerful media organisations, controlled by business groups linked to two tycoons reported to have been in the losing consortium, have launched a bitter attack on the Svyazinvest deal. They have branded it a shadowy affair between state officials and financial magnates, directing their strongest fire against Nemtsov.
The minister hit back by blasting the losers of the auction as "bandit capitalists".

The row, especially the blistering condemnations of the sale and of Nemtsov on television and on newspapers' front pages, made clear that an alliance of rival magnates who combined their money and media muscle to secure Yeltsin's re-election last year was at an end.
The president himself has yet to comment directly on the scandal.
